name: BGA

claims.claim_text: Ball grid array and chip-scale packages are cheaper to manufacture than leaded packages because the ball connects directly to the substrate and no bond wires are required.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't have to put the bond wires in then because the ball is directly on the back side
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: Wire bonding is the throughput constraint it removes: each wire is placed individually, and a second per part is the difference between ten thousand and a hundred thousand chips a day.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can only get, you know, 10,000 chips a day instead of, you know, 100,000
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: A chip-scale package is named for being essentially no larger than the bare die, with the balls landing on the top layer of the die's own metallisation once it is flipped over.
claims.quote_verbatim: the package is essentially no bigger than the bare die
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A land grid array is the same arrangement without the balls, using flat pads, which suits applications constrained in height because the ball's contribution to the vertical dimension is removed.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't have to sacrifice the Z, the delta Z contributed by the balls
claims.speaker: Ming Zhang

claims.claim_text: Ball pitch is the parameter that determines everything downstream: a pitch of 1.27 millimetres is generously wide, most contemporary parts sit at 0.8 millimetres or below, and 0.4 millimetres is genuinely difficult.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the BGA's these days is 0.8
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Parts at 0.25 and 0.4 millimetre pitch cannot be escaped on an inexpensive standard prototype board process at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: you just literally can't use some of the parts that are out there these days that are like 0.25, 0.4 millimeter pitch BGAs
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A pooled prototype fabrication service could handle a one millimetre pitch part without difficulty, with anything finer described as pushing the process.
claims.quote_verbatim: So yes, you can do BGA is one millimeter is no problem. Once it gets smaller than that, it's, it's pushing it.
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: To let customers place 0.8 millimetre pitch parts, that service raised its four-layer design rules to five thousandths of an inch trace and space with a ten thousandth drill and a four thousandth annular ring, which is just enough to squeak through.
claims.quote_verbatim: it has five, five, uh, trace spacing, and then it has, um, 10 mil drill and four mil annular ring
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: Those published numbers are the fabricator's guaranteed values rather than enforced limits, so designs violating them are sometimes submitted and built by accident.
claims.quote_verbatim: these design rules that I have with my fabs are, uh, uh, are the guaranteed numbers
claims.speaker: Laen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Laen - Purple PCB Philosophy

claims.claim_text: A service offering an eight thousandth minimum drill and five thousandth annular ring is respectable for general work but not adequate for small ball grid arrays.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's actually pretty tidy but it's not necessarily great for people that are trying to do little BGAs
claims.speaker: Jonathan Hirschman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jonathan Hirschman of PCB:NG

claims.claim_text: At 0.4 millimetre pitch, a part with three rows of balls can still be escaped and manufactured cheaply; beyond three rows the design requires laser-drilled vias, on the order of a 0.15 to 0.2 millimetre drill.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you've got a three row 0.4 millimeter pitch one, you can actually route it out and you can get it manufactured cheaply.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jason Kridner - Bonafide BeagleBoard Bionomics

claims.claim_text: An open hardware platform deliberately moved from 0.4 to 0.8 millimetre ball pitch so that users could fabricate and build their own variants, since a fine-pitch part makes that impossible.
claims.quote_verbatim: They've gone from 0.4 millimetre pin-pitch balls on their BGA devices. They're using a 0.8 millimetre pin-pitch
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard successors, CAD & Robots - Haussmannized Halloween Hypostrophe

claims.claim_text: Fine pitch also raises board cost directly, because the tolerances on solder mask registration and etching all tighten with the pitch.
claims.quote_verbatim: Your boards are more expensive to manufacture because the tolerances are all tighter on the solder mass
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: BeagleBoard successors, CAD & Robots - Haussmannized Halloween Hypostrophe

claims.claim_text: Escape routing, not soldering, is the property that decides whether a package is usable on an ordinary board: a three-row 256-ball part at 1.27 millimetre pitch can have every pin escaped on the top layer with six thousandth trace and space, which puts a complete Linux-capable device on a four-layer board.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can escape all 256 pins with a 6 mil space and trace
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The significance of that property is routinely underestimated by designers evaluating a part.
claims.quote_verbatim: People don't realize what a big deal escaping BGA's is.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: High ball counts force layer counts: a thousand-pin part needs on the order of eight layers purely to route the signals out.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got this thousand pin monster BGA on there, you know, big FPGA thing, right? You need eight layers just to route that bastard out
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: CAD programs, Systems Design and Renewable Energy

claims.claim_text: A six-hundred-pin part likewise dictated an eight-layer board with no possibility of fewer.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because you need to fan out the 600 pin BGA. Yes. Just no way you can do it on any fewer.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A designer constrained to four layers finds that searching for new silicon in leaded packages returns almost nothing, and the parts that remain are ball grid arrays needing six or eight layers to fan out.
claims.quote_verbatim: The only thing you can find is BGAs which need six or eight layers to fan out all the pins
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: The pin count required by a device can be wildly out of proportion to the pins actually used: a design needing only serial in and serial out was forced onto a twelve-hundred-pin part, with a twelve-layer board to route it, and the pins are where the cost sits.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only chip that did the job was a 1,200-pin BGA
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: Careful pin assignment can keep a large part on a modest board: a 256-ball package with memory on the opposite side of the board was routed on four layers, with two of those layers given over to power and ground.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've got the 256-ball BGA on one side and I've got the SD RAM on the other side
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: Pin assignment is where the difficulty concentrates in such a design, because the requirement is to get a specific pin to a specific destination through the available layers.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you talk about pin assignment, that's where its hair is on the printer wiring board
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: An 81-ball part at 0.4 millimetre pitch is specified for a high-density interconnect process using via-in-pad with roughly 0.2 millimetre vias on a 0.1 millimetre drill, filled and plated, which is prohibitively expensive at prototype quantities.
claims.quote_verbatim: the official recommendation is to use via in pad with, you know, 0.2 millimeter vias and like a 0.1 millimeter drill
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Where that process was unaffordable, the workarounds used were routing over unused pads and covering them with solder mask to reach buried signals, and placing a via in the centre of a two-by-two group of pads.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had no choice but to take, you know, two by two quads of pads and put a via in the middle of them
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: More signals were escaped by narrowing the outer row of pads to 0.1 millimetre and elongating them to 0.35 millimetre, preserving roughly the same surface area for the ball to wick to while opening a gap for traces to pass between them.
claims.quote_verbatim: I took the outer pads of the BGA and I squished them down to 0.1 millimeter and then I elongated them
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: The pill-shaped pad gains no area over the original circle; the gain is entirely in the reduced width, which is what allows a track to escape between pads.
claims.quote_verbatim: the elongated pad, the neck down pad is actually a smaller width than the original circular pad
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The designer's own recommendation after doing it was that others should not repeat it: a larger package, and specifically 0.8 millimetre pitch, is dramatically easier and escapes by conventional means on four layers.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would not recommend using the same FPGA package
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Yield is a further consequence of fine pitch: a small board built around such a package had a low enough assembly yield that its maker would only produce more in bulk quantities.
claims.quote_verbatim: the yield on these boards was low because of the BGA package
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Solder mask can be pulled slightly over the pad edge to help align the ball and to help the solder fill correctly, a technique used where via-in-pad is unavoidable because of density.
claims.quote_verbatim: you might close the solder mask a little bit over the pad to help with the ball alignment
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The ball's specified size is its widest dimension, while the actual contact area on the pad is smaller because the ball is a sphere that necks down where it meets the pad.
claims.quote_verbatim: the maximum width of the ball, but usually the actual contact of the ball on the pad is smaller
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Whether pads are defined by the solder mask opening or by the copper is a genuine choice, and one worth testing empirically before committing a design.
claims.quote_verbatim: do we do solder mask-defined or copper-defined pads
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: The package is self-aligning during reflow: surface tension pulls the part into position over the pads, which makes placement accuracy less critical than it appears.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's self-aligning. The surface tension, you know, pulls the chip in line
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The single most important variable in hand-pasting is using too little rather than too much: a small amount of paste is enough to make a connection, whereas excess causes shorts beneath the package that cannot be found visually.
claims.quote_verbatim: you only have to get a small amount of paste on there to get at least a connection
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Shorts under the part are the characteristic failure of over-pasting, and they are invisible once the part is down.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't want shorts under your BGA
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Self-alignment weakens as the package grows: a ball grid array is heavy enough that surface tension helps less, whereas a wafer-level chip-scale part is so small and light that it behaves more like soldering a resistor.
claims.quote_verbatim: bull grid arrays start to get, um, big enough that the surface tension doesn't help you as much
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Where paste can be screened through a decent stencil, the package is among the easier components to solder precisely because of that surface tension.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's actually not that hard. It's probably one of the easier components to solder if you know how to screen solder paste

claims.claim_text: Laser-cut polyimide stencils have a floor of about five thousandths of an inch in every direction, below which the plastic melts back over the opening instead of cutting through, though people routinely use that limit for fine-pitch parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: the minimum feature size is it has to be at least five mils in in all directions
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: Stainless steel stencils are the better choice for the same work: they are flatter, dimensionally consistent, align more precisely and release paste better, producing fewer bridges and stray solder balls than film.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're less likely to get bridges, solder balls, all sorts of things like that because, um, the metal's more consistent
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: The economic case for the better stencil is rework avoided: a single bridged joint costs hours, and a bridge hidden underneath the package is worse still.
claims.quote_verbatim: if it's underneath the BGA, it's like even worse
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent of OSHstencils

claims.claim_text: Paste application is the process step that limits assembly quality, and hand stencilling is inconsistent enough that pressure variation leaves individual pads without paste to reflow.
claims.quote_verbatim: you do your pressure a little bit wrong. You know, one, one pad's not going to get any paste

claims.claim_text: A modern automated printer with an under-stencil wipe improves paste quality enough to make consistently smaller parts feasible, and a contemporary placement machine handling thirteen thousand placements an hour will place very fine ball grid arrays.
claims.quote_verbatim: it can do like 13,000 placements an hour can do BGAs, uh, very fine BGAs

claims.claim_text: Benchtop assembly machines aimed at prototype work cover 0402 passives and 0.4 millimetre pitch leaded parts, with users reporting good results placing 0.5 millimetre pitch ball grid arrays.
claims.quote_verbatim: people say they've had great luck with 0.5 millimeter pitch BGA
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Vapour phase reflow includes a hold at around a hundred and twenty degrees Celsius to vaporise residual fluid off the board and out from underneath components, so no droplets are left between the balls.
claims.quote_verbatim: we try to um take the pcb to 120 degrees celsius
claims.speaker: Saber Kaygusuz

claims.claim_text: X-ray inspection is useful for the obvious defects such as a short between adjacent balls, but is not effective at finding an intermittent or merely poor connection.
claims.quote_verbatim: I think it is useful for like really obvious, like you have a short between balls
claims.speaker: Joe Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: A small operation without x-ray equipment instead controls the paste process, budgets for a failure rate on the order of one in ten thousand and discards or reflows the failures rather than diagnosing them.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'd get your process right so that you're going to have one fire in 10,000
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Boundary scan through the debug interface verifies that every ball on a large package is connected and not shorted to its neighbours, which substitutes for x-ray equipment where none is available.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can make sure that your thousand pin BGA, that every one of those pins is actually connected to the ball by, by doing a boundary scan
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Mounting the package on a flexible circuit with no stiffener allows the joints to be inspected through the translucent film from the back, showing every ball directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you put a BGA on a flex PCB, uh, with no stiffener, you can look through the back
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen

claims.claim_text: Without inspection equipment full verification is impractical, but electrical test is frequently sufficient in practice, and the package is not inherently difficult to work with.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you can just electrically test, that's often enough
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen

claims.claim_text: Computed-tomography inspection reconstructs the assembly in three dimensions and re-slices through it, revealing detail such as voiding inside the solder joints.
claims.quote_verbatim: it actually had like, remember I showed you like the, the BGA balls, like you could actually see voiding underneath
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The part has to be held at a deliberately non-orthogonal angle during such a scan, because viewing straight along a row of balls means the nearest ball blocks the path to the ones behind it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the front ball would basically block the
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: In hot-air rework the temperature is controlled by hand through nozzle distance and angle rather than by the setting on the station, with a quarter of an inch of nozzle movement worth roughly thirty degrees at the board.
claims.quote_verbatim: you move the nozzle a quarter of an inch away from the board, you'll see a 30 degree drop
claims.speaker: Louis Rossmann

claims.claim_text: The variables that actually determine the outcome are the element temperature, the airflow setting, the nozzle size and angle, the surrounding components and how well the board sinks heat.
claims.quote_verbatim: not only the temperature of the element, but the airflow, the size
claims.speaker: Louis Rossmann

claims.claim_text: A thermocouple placed on the part is used when replacing a very large package of several hundred balls, and is not practical for smaller work where hand control suffices.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're replacing like, you know, a 900 ball, a large BGA, you need to do that
claims.speaker: Louis Rossmann

claims.claim_text: Large processors and graphics parts require a preheater under the board with hot air above, or a professional rework station; a ninety-ball part or one with 0.25 millimetre balls is achievable with ordinary hand rework equipment.
claims.quote_verbatim: a 90 ball or a BGA with like 0.25 millimeter balls that that's doable
claims.speaker: Louis Rossmann

claims.claim_text: Replacing a very large package is uneconomic even where it is possible, because replacement parts of that class come only from doubtful sources and a forty-minute operation that fails leaves nothing to show for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: If I spend 40 minutes replacing a chip and either the chip is bad or the board is bad
claims.speaker: Louis Rossmann

claims.claim_text: Becoming comfortable with a microscope is what removes the difficulty, since tilting the board reveals the balls underneath the package and makes the joint quality directly visible.
claims.quote_verbatim: A lot of it is becoming comfortable with a microscope because once you can actually see what you're doing, it's not scary.
claims.speaker: Louis Rossmann

claims.claim_text: Rework skill decays without regular use, to the point that an engineer who has not used hot air for several months practises before attempting a real part.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I haven't like used my hot air gun for like three or six months to actually, you know, remove a chip or do something, it's like, I almost have to practice again
claims.speaker: Louis Rossmann

claims.claim_text: The corresponding advice is to build soldering skill on low-risk work rather than on the board that has to work tomorrow, because running a bodge wire out from under a package is a high-risk operation to attempt for the first time under pressure.
claims.quote_verbatim: try to practice soldering with low risk projects
claims.speaker: Greg Davill

claims.claim_text: Soldering to an individual pad of a one millimetre pitch package by hand is achievable, and is in fact easier than doing the same on a 0.5 millimetre pitch quad flat pack.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's actually harder to solder onto a 0.5mm pitch quad flat pack or something as a dead bug, you know, than it is a 1mm pitch BGA
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Prototyping, Machining & Accelerators- Mugwumps Mulling Milling

claims.claim_text: Paste application is the skill that decides hand-assembly yield at these sizes: on one fine-pitch design three boards were assembled and one worked.
claims.quote_verbatim: i've assembled three boards and one of them worked
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Like a steam engine in your house

claims.claim_text: A 0.35 millimetre pitch wafer-level part was placed on a six-layer service with via-in-pad by working at exactly the process minimum of 0.25 millimetres, which requires the layout grid to be constructed to match or the fabricator's checks reject it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the via and pad was the exact amount of uh distance like the the exact minimum distance
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Like a steam engine in your house

claims.claim_text: At that pitch not all rows of the array can be used, and on that design roughly forty of the sixty-four available signals were brought out.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't use all three rows of the of the csp
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Like a steam engine in your house

claims.claim_text: A stencil ordered alongside a board can be cut from an earlier revision than the one finally fabricated, so the stencil no longer matches the board it was bought for.
claims.quote_verbatim: they made the stencil of the first design and they just they set it and forget it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Like a steam engine in your house

claims.claim_text: Redesigning to escape the package is a legitimate outcome: one board was reworked to move from a ball grid array footprint to a leaded package specifically so it could be soldered and desoldered reliably by hand, after a previous version yielded one working board out of five.
claims.quote_verbatim: That required a BGA footprint. And now I'm able to get it down to a QFN
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Designers who intend to assemble and rework their own boards select parts accordingly: one project chose the largest FPGA available in a non-ball-grid package to preserve hand rework, accepting the loss of hardware multipliers and compensating with different signal-processing algorithms.
claims.quote_verbatim: it had the most pins of any FPGA that was not in a ball grid package
claims.speaker: Matt Ettus
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Matt Ettus - Quality Quadrature Quidam

claims.claim_text: Keeping a design assemblable with a soldering iron is a stated design constraint for some engineers, who choose a large leaded package where one exists and accept its physical size, resorting to a ball grid array only where no alternative is available.
claims.quote_verbatim: I like to make my designs, you know, something you can assemble with an iron
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: The contrary view is that a wide-pitch ball grid array is preferable to a very fine pitch leaded package, since a 0.8 millimetre pitch array is easier to work with than a 0.4 millimetre pitch quad flat pack carrying a large number of pins.
claims.quote_verbatim: give me a fricking 0.8 millimeter pitch BGA any day of the week compared to that

claims.claim_text: Higher-performance application processors sit at 0.5 or 0.65 millimetre pitch, which places them in a different category of layout difficulty from the parts a hobbyist would normally attempt.
claims.quote_verbatim: 0.5 millimeter pitch BGA for most of them, 0.65 for some of them

claims.claim_text: The reservation held against the package by designers who avoid it is visibility: a fault cannot be diagnosed without removing the whole part.
claims.quote_verbatim: I avoid BGA. I think it's because of the visibility thing.

claims.claim_text: Newly released parts are increasingly available only in packages too fine to use on an ordinary process, and the direction of travel across the industry is towards chip-scale packages, so declining to learn them progressively locks a designer out of current silicon.
claims.quote_verbatim: otherwise you start to lock yourself out of certain technologies and certain chips
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The same constraint applied a decade earlier: specialised parts available only in micro ball grid array made small production runs impractical.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're trying to make a hundred of something, you know, and the chip's only available in a micro BGA, then you're, you know, you're pretty much screwed
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: These packages are designed for high-volume production where the setup cost of getting the process right is amortised, which is what makes them awkward for anyone building in small quantities.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're, they're designed for high volume, you know, mass produced
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Substituting a switching regulator can cascade into a package change from a leaded part to a ball grid array or wafer-level package, which in turn forces blind and buried vias and a much larger qualification effort.
claims.quote_verbatim: you might be moving from a QFN package or something bigger like a BGA or a WLCSP package. So the really small ones that trigger having to go to blind and buried vias.
claims.speaker: Dave Young

claims.claim_text: Where the array is fully populated, giving up top-layer routing costs roughly one and a half pin rows of escape; the preferred remedy is blind and buried vias rather than simply adding layers, because through vias consume routing space on every layer they pass.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'd probably lose one and a half uh pin layers of routing if you didn't use the top
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The manual effort scales with ball count: a thousand-pin part with every pin in use means roughly a thousand traces and a thousand vias to place, multiplied by however many times the routing is torn up and redone.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's a thousand traces you've got to place. That's probably a thousand vias you've got to place.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: That effort is what makes autorouting economically interesting for these parts, with a topological router that lays traces as a person would rather than on a grid able to route a package in hours where manual work takes days.
claims.quote_verbatim: if this thing can route a BGA package in two hours where it might take you, you know, two days
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Autorouter, Datasheets & Obscure Chips - Cloddish Collegiate Conversations

claims.claim_text: Dense multi-package boards have been laid out successfully in hobbyist-tier tools, but time spent compensating for a tool's limitations is time not spent designing, which is the argument against pushing a tool past its comfortable range.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you spend too much time trying to compensate for the inadequacies of a CAD tool
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Discussing The Open Hardware Summit With MightyOhm - Ostrobogulous Openness Occasion

claims.claim_text: The escape problem is also an architectural constraint on silicon: with a one millimetre pitch package only so many traces can leave the part, whereas an on-chip wire may be a tenth of a micron wide and thousands can run in parallel, which is why a larger single die gives a super-linear gain over many small chips.
claims.quote_verbatim: let's say you have a BGA with a one millimeter pitch. There are only so many traces you can fit on that board.
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: Connecting two packaged chips means stepping a signal up from a transistor of a few tens of nanometres, through a die pad of tens of microns, a package trace, a half-millimetre ball, and an eight-thousandth board trace, then back down the same ladder — a change of roughly a millionfold in each direction, which is the argument for integrating dies into one package.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're going from a 14 nanometer transistor to a 70 micron die pad
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Ball count alone does not determine difficulty: a 676-ball part at one millimetre pitch is straightforward, while a much smaller part at fine pitch is not.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a 676 ball part. But it has a really easy pitch. It's a one-millimeter pitch.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Differing thermal expansion coefficients between the board, the silicon and the overmould leave the solder balls carrying the resulting stress as the assembly heats, which is why reliability analysis asks why a ball at a particular position fails and uses heat-transfer and finite-element modelling to answer it.
claims.quote_verbatim: the poor solder is in the middle and it's got to deal with the fact that the board is expanding maybe more than the chip is

claims.claim_text: A design-review service can flag layout hazards specific to the package, such as a ball grid array placed close enough to a capacitor to cause thermal shadowing during reflow.
claims.quote_verbatim: that BGA is going to have some shadowing, some heat shadowing because it's a little bit too close to one of the caps
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Custom test sockets for these packages run to thousands of dollars, must align perfectly across every contact, and degrade measured performance, so a distortion figure taken through a socket may look poor for reasons that have nothing to do with the device.
claims.quote_verbatim: those sockets can run to thousands of dollars
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Where only one part on a board requires fine-pitch capability, the entire board area is manufactured to that tolerance and the rest of the design carries the cost of that single chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: everything else is basically carrying the cost of this one chip
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The remedy is to isolate the difficult part on a small module with castellated edges or a board-to-board connector, since a one-inch square high-specification board plus interconnects is cheaper than manufacturing a large board to the same tolerance.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's cheaper to get like a tiny little one inch by one inch board made, put the BGA on there and have pastellated edges
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Escaping a package on four layers rather than six, and at a coarser trace-and-space class, opens the job to cheaper fabricators and is worth designing for deliberately.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you can escape your BGA on four layers, you do it because it's going to be cheaper
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A commercially bought module carries the same benefit with the tight tolerances and often the regulatory certification already paid for, at the cost of the module's price premium.
claims.quote_verbatim: it might have, you know, super tight tolerance, you know, and then it's also pre-certified
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A system-in-package integrates processor, memory and support components into a wide-pitch ball grid array, so a complete Linux system becomes one part soldered down with no memory routing or controlled-impedance work required, at a price close to that of a whole single-board computer.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you want Linux on a board with a single thing soldered down, that's pretty sweet
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: One such module was deliberately specified at 0.8 millimetre pitch and chosen for ease of routing, so that no expensive stack-up or dense via structure is needed to break the package out, and the underlying processor can be substituted behind a fixed footprint.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's 0.8 millimeter, so it's pretty standard BGA pin pitch. So we don't have to use highly expensive stack-ups
claims.speaker: Lukas Henkel
claims.episode_title: Compact High Speed Design with Lukas Henkel

claims.claim_text: The same reasoning drove an earlier product: a module carrying the ball grid array FPGA meant customers building the board themselves never had to solder it, and moving to a single hand-assembled board required switching to a leaded FPGA and dropping the features that the larger part had supported.
claims.quote_verbatim: I used an FPGA module that had the BGA FPGA on it so that they didn't have to do that soldering
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin O'Flynn - Aspirated Adamantine Attacks

claims.claim_text: Packaging is where the visible innovation now sits rather than in board technology, with cross-sections of a system-in-package showing stacked dies, tiny internal boards and package-on-package memory forming a three-dimensional structure.
claims.quote_verbatim: inside that it's got several chips that are stacked with other tinier pcbs in there
claims.speaker: Eric Schlaepfer
claims.episode_title: Open Circuits with Eric Schlaepfer and Windell Oskay

claims.claim_text: Stacked package-on-package memory combined with fine ball pitch is what gave one widely used board its reputation for being difficult to assemble.
claims.quote_verbatim: the OMAP 3 has the stacked memory on top of the package, the package on package
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeff Keyzer and Jason Kridner - Bonafide BeagleBoard Bionomics

claims.claim_text: Wafer-level chip-scale parts are small ball grid arrays produced directly at wafer level, and taping out into one requires additional information about the packaging and how the balls are bonded, which an intermediary service can absorb on the designer's behalf.
claims.quote_verbatim: a wafer-level chip scale package. So they're like little BGA.
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: Fine pitch appears even on very small parts: a three-by-three millimetre programmable device carries forty-nine balls at 0.4 millimetre pitch with thirty-three usable signals.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a 49 ball BGA with 33 available IOs
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A wafer chip-scale part measuring 1.6 by 1.6 millimetres carried a three-by-three matrix of pads with the centre position omitted because the sensing element occupied that area.
claims.quote_verbatim: 1.6 millimeter by 1.6 millimeter wafer chip scale package BGA
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Drill size and annular ring are what drive fabrication price sharply upward on a small four-layer board carrying a 0.5 millimetre pitch part, to the point that low-cost fabricators quote thousands for the tightest values.
claims.quote_verbatim: the drill size and the. Annual ring, if it gets too small, the price just jumps
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Signal escape from the package is what limits how many general-purpose pins a low-technology board can expose, and is the constraint cited for not bringing more out on a widely produced single-board computer.
claims.quote_verbatim: the signal escape on the BGA is obviously a tricky thing given we've gone for a fairly low tech PCB
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eben Upton - Morbus Moilsome MakerFaire

claims.claim_text: An image sensor in a package designed for mobile telephones forced a design that would otherwise have fitted on two layers onto a four-layer service, purely because the two-layer process could not hold the fine trace and space needed to route the part out.
claims.quote_verbatim: the pin pitch is so small that you can't route out
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Dual-row packages with a large central thermal pad present the same escape problem, with the vendor's suggested layout calling for blind and buried vias that raise board cost substantially.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's called an AQFN, but what it is is like a dual row, like tiny BGA with a huge thermal pad in the middle
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A leaded package with configurable peripheral routing is preferable to a fine-pitch ball grid array where the design does not actually need a large number of pins.
claims.quote_verbatim: rather than having a BGA with super fine small balls on it, you've got this one QFN package
claims.speaker: Daryl Tewksbury
claims.episode_title: Outdoor Laser Projection & Object Mapping with Daryl Tewksbury

claims.claim_text: The package was not approved for use in flight hardware until the late two thousands.
claims.quote_verbatim: that BGAs were approved for flight

claims.claim_text: Milling a board in house can reach these packages: a spring-mounted engraving tip with a very small point allowed leadless parts and light ball grid array work, including four and six ball parts at around 0.35 millimetre pitch.
claims.quote_verbatim: That allowed me to do QFN and some very light BGA stuff eventually.
claims.speaker: Mike Grover

claims.claim_text: A laser-cut polyimide stencil can be produced for essentially any package including ball and land grid arrays, with high pin count leaded packages presenting more difficulty than the arrays.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can cut any packet that's out there. BGA, LGA, tiny QFN stuff.
claims.speaker: Ryan O'Hara
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: A ball grid array in the assembly is one of the standard reasons a designer outsources a board rather than building it themselves.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've got to get my BGA in place. I can't do this by hand.
claims.speaker: Chris Church
claims.episode_title: An interview with Macrofab - Macro Manufacturing Mechanization

claims.claim_text: Prototyping methods that stop short of a professionally fabricated board are ruled out by the packages in current use, since a ball grid array has to be reflowed and cannot be worked by hand-etched means.
claims.quote_verbatim: You've got BGA parts that you have to reflow.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Ariel Briner of Cartesian Co
